chapter: Chapter 5: Universal Franchise and India's Electoral System
source: NCERT Class 8 Social Science (Exploring Society: India and Beyond — Part 1)

questions.question: What does the term 'franchise' or 'suffrage' mean in a democracy?
options: The right to vote granted by the Constitution or government
The right to collect taxes from citizens
The right to form a business company
questions.explanation: Franchise (also called suffrage) refers to the right to vote granted to citizens by the Constitution or government.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for elections based on Universal Adult Franchise?
questions.explanation: Article 326 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are based on universal adult suffrage.

questions.question: What is the minimum age required for an Indian citizen to vote in elections?
questions.explanation: Every Indian citizen aged 18 years and above has the right to vote under Universal Adult Franchise.

questions.question: In which year did India lower the minimum voting age from 21 years to 18 years?
questions.explanation: India reduced the minimum voting age from 21 to 18 in 1988 (via the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act), empowering millions of young citizens.

questions.question: Who remarked in the Constituent Assembly in November 1949 that India adopted adult franchise with 'abundant faith in the common man'?
questions.explanation: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar made this famous statement in November 1949 during the Constituent Assembly Debates.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of Indians were allowed to vote before Independence?
questions.explanation: Before Independence, franchise was not universal and only around 13 per cent of Indians had the right to vote.

questions.question: In 1947, what was India's approximate overall literacy rate and women's literacy rate respectively?
questions.explanation: In 1947, India's literacy rate was about 14 per cent overall and only about 8 per cent among women, yet the Constitution makers boldly granted universal franchise.

questions.question: In contrast to India granting women voting rights from the beginning, in which year did women in Switzerland get the right to vote?
questions.explanation: India was among the early nations to grant women voting rights from the very start, whereas women in Switzerland were given the right to vote only in 1971.

questions.question: Under what legal condition can an adult Indian citizen be barred from voting?
options: If they do not own property or land
If they are found guilty of committing certain serious crimes
If they have not completed high school
If they live in a rural area
questions.explanation: While voting is universal regardless of wealth or education, a citizen can be legally barred from voting if convicted of certain serious crimes.

questions.question: What does the principle of 'one person, one vote, one value' mean under Universal Adult Franchise?
options: Citizens can vote on behalf of their family members
Every adult citizen gets one vote and every vote carries equal value
questions.explanation: Universal adult franchise guarantees that every adult citizen has one vote, all votes have equal value, and no one can vote on another's behalf.

questions.question: Approximately how many elected representatives serve in India's more than 250,000 local government bodies, and how many of them are women?
questions.explanation: India has 3.1 million elected representatives—1.3 million of them women—across more than 250,000 local government bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT determine a citizen's right to vote in India?
options: Registration on the voter list of a constituency
questions.explanation: Wealth, education, caste, religion, creed, race, or gender do not affect a citizen's right to vote in India.

questions.question: What is a 'constituency' in an electoral system?
options: A list of laws passed by Parliament
A meeting of political party leaders
A machine used to count ballot papers
An area whose voters elect a representative to a legislative body
questions.explanation: A constituency is a defined geographical area whose registered voters elect a representative to a legislative body such as the Lok Sabha or State Assembly.

questions.question: In the context of governance, how does the NCERT textbook define a 'system'?
options: A temporary committee formed after elections
A group of interconnected or interdependent elements working together for a common purpose
An informal group of voters in a village
A single law passed by the President
questions.explanation: A system is defined as a group of interconnected or interdependent elements that work together to achieve a common purpose or function.

questions.question: Why does Universal Adult Franchise make elected representatives accountable?
options: Because only ministers can question them
Because citizens can vote them out in the next election if they fail to perform
Because representatives are appointed for life
questions.explanation: Because every adult citizen holds the power to vote, elected representatives remain answerable to the electorate and can be voted out if they do not serve the people.

questions.question: Approximately how many voters were eligible to vote in India's 2024 Lok Sabha General Elections?
questions.explanation: In the summer of 2024, over 968 million Indian citizens were eligible to exercise their franchise across 543 Lok Sabha constituencies.

questions.question: According to the NCERT chapter, India's eligible voter population is about how many times the population of the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: To highlight the massive scale of Indian elections, the textbook notes that India's eligible voter population is fifteen times the population of the United Kingdom.

questions.question: In terms of geographical area, India is approximately how many times larger than France?
questions.explanation: India's geographical area is six times larger than France, adding significant logistical diversity to conducting elections.

questions.question: What landmark accessibility measure was introduced for the first time in India's 2024 General Elections?
options: Home voting facility for the elderly and persons with disabilities
questions.explanation: In 2024, for the first time, senior citizens (elderly) and persons with disabilities could cast their votes from home.

questions.question: Which assistive measures has the ECI introduced to help visually impaired and mobility-challenged voters?
options: Braille-enabled voter cards, ramps, wheelchairs, and app-based assistance requests
Separate election dates for cities only
questions.explanation: The ECI provides Braille-enabled voter cards, ramps, wheelchairs, and app-based assistance to remove barriers for voters with disabilities.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of eligible voters did NOT exercise their right to vote in the 2024 General Elections?
questions.explanation: About 34 per cent of eligible voters did not cast their votes in the 2024 elections, highlighting the need for greater voter awareness and participation.

questions.question: The Uttaramerur inscriptions, which describe a transparent ancient Indian method of selecting representatives, date back to which century?
questions.explanation: The 10th-century Uttaramerur inscriptions (in Tamil Nadu) document a transparent democratic selection process for local representatives.

questions.question: In the selection process described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions, what material were eligible candidates' names written on?
questions.explanation: Candidates' names were written on fragments of palm leaves, placed inside a sealed pot, and drawn randomly in public by a young boy.

questions.question: Why did the respected individual in the Uttaramerur selection process show his empty hands to the public before reading out names?
options: To ensure complete transparency and prove there was no cheating or hidden palm leaf
To signal the end of the harvest season
To ask for donations from villagers
To bless the newly elected king
questions.explanation: Showing empty hands to the public guaranteed fairness and transparency so no one could accuse the reader of concealing or swapping a palm leaf.

questions.question: Who was the first voter in independent India's general elections of 1951?
questions.explanation: Shyam Saran Negi, a school teacher from Himachal Pradesh, was the first voter in India's 1951 general elections and even voted at age 100 in 2017.

questions.question: Shyam Saran Negi, India's first voter in 1951, belonged to which Indian state and profession?
questions.explanation: Shyam Saran Negi was a school teacher in Himachal Pradesh who cast the first vote in independent India's general elections in 1951.

questions.question: Roughly how many polling stations were set up across India during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: Over 1 million polling stations were established across India to serve more than 968 million voters in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.

questions.question: To ensure 'no voter is left behind', what remarkable step has India's electoral system even undertaken in remote areas?
options: Required remote voters to travel to Delhi
Allowed village heads to vote for everyone
Set up a dedicated polling station even for a single eligible voter
questions.explanation: Electoral officials travel to remote locations and have even organised a polling station for a single woman voter to uphold universal franchise.

questions.question: What voting facility is available for specific categories of voters (such as service personnel on election duty or essential services) who cannot visit their polling station?
questions.explanation: Postal voting (postal ballots) allows specific eligible categories of voters who cannot be physically present at their booth to cast their votes.

questions.question: Figure 5.3 in the NCERT chapter depicts a historic Women's Suffrage Parade held in which country and year?
questions.explanation: Figure 5.3 shows the 1913 Women's Suffrage Parade in the USA, illustrating how women in many countries had to fight long struggles for voting rights.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School Grade 8 Class Representative election caselet, who were the three contesting candidates?
questions.explanation: Ahmed, Gurmat, and Ravi contested the Grade 8 Class Representative election at Suryodaya School.

questions.question: Who served as the Election Officer for the Grade 8 Class Representative election at Suryodaya School?
questions.explanation: Ms. Usha, the class teacher, was appointed as the Election Officer to organise and conduct the election fairly and transparently.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School election, what did Gurmat promise to introduce if elected?
options: More timetable space for music, theatre, and visual arts
A system of peer coaching and mutual support to help classmates learn better
questions.explanation: Gurmat proposed creating a system of peer coaching and mutual support so all classmates could learn better.

questions.question: How did Ravi campaign for his proposal to expand the arts curriculum in the Suryodaya School election?
options: By holding a lunchtime music performance
By putting up posters on classroom walls
questions.explanation: Ahmed put up posters, Gurmat used the noticeboard and spoke to classmates, while Ravi held a lunchtime music performance.

questions.question: Why did Ms. Usha prepare a special ballot paper in Braille during the class election?
options: To ensure Neha, a visually impaired student, could vote independently and secretly
To make the election look more decorative
questions.explanation: Providing a Braille ballot paper for Neha ensured inclusive and secret voting, mirroring the ECI's accessibility measures.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a 'secret ballot'?
options: To keep every voter's choice private so they can vote freely without fear or pressure
To speed up the printing of ballots
To allow teachers to see who voted for whom
questions.explanation: A secret ballot ensures that no one knows whom a voter chose, protecting voters from intimidation, pressure, or bias.

questions.question: Why did Ms. Usha call Ms. Sheeba from the next class during the vote counting?
options: To act as an independent witness to ensure fair and transparent counting
To cast an extra tie-breaking vote
questions.explanation: Having Ms. Sheeba witness the counting ensured transparency and fairness, just like observers and agents in real elections.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School election, why was one of the ballot papers declared invalid?
questions.explanation: One ballot paper was not marked with an 'X' next to any candidate's name, so it was declared invalid.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School election, Gurmat won with 12 votes out of 33 cast (Ahmed 8, Ravi 10). Which electoral principle does this illustrate?
options: First-Past-The-Post, where the highest vote-getter wins even without 50% of votes
questions.explanation: Gurmat won with 12 out of 33 votes (less than 50%), illustrating India's First-Past-The-Post system where simply getting the most votes wins.

questions.question: What does the acronym NOTA stand for in Indian elections?
questions.explanation: NOTA stands for 'None Of The Above', giving voters the right to reject all contesting candidates.

questions.question: What happens to the election result if voters choose the NOTA option?
options: The entire election is immediately cancelled
It does not change the result, but sends a message that voters want better choices
The Election Commission appoints a candidate directly
questions.explanation: As explained in the NCERT chapter, NOTA does not change the outcome of the election, but serves as a quiet yet powerful message demanding better candidates.

questions.question: After Gurmat won the class election, how did Ahmed and Ravi respond?
options: They congratulated her and offered to support her
They demanded a recount every week
questions.explanation: Ahmed and Ravi congratulated Gurmat and offered their support, demonstrating healthy democratic sportsmanship.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School election, what was Ahmed's main campaign promise?
options: Improving the cleanliness of the classrooms and the playground
questions.explanation: Ahmed promised to improve the cleanliness of both the classrooms and the playground, and campaigned by putting up posters.

questions.question: How did Ms. Usha keep the ballot box secure between voting and counting?
options: She collected the ballots in a box and sealed it until the counting session
She left it open on her desk
She counted each vote loudly as students voted
She handed it to one of the candidates
questions.explanation: Sealing the ballot box until counting prevents tampering and mirrors official ECI protocols.

questions.question: If Suryodaya School formed a special school-level council elected only by the Class Representatives, what type of election would that be?
questions.explanation: When elected representatives (Class Reps) vote to choose members of a higher council, it is an indirect election—just like Rajya Sabha elections.

questions.question: What kind of body is the Election Commission of India (ECI)?
options: A committee of the Lok Sabha Speaker
A department under the Prime Minister's Office
questions.explanation: The ECI is an independent constitutional body responsible for conducting free and fair elections in India.

questions.question: In which year was the Election Commission of India (ECI) established?
questions.explanation: The Election Commission of India was established in 1950 (on 25 January 1950).

questions.question: When were the first general elections held in independent India?
questions.explanation: Independent India's first general elections were held in 1951–1952 under the supervision of the ECI.

questions.question: Which of the following elections is NOT conducted by the Election Commission of India (ECI)?
options: Gram Panchayat and Urban Local Body elections
questions.explanation: Elections to Gram Panchayats and Urban Local Bodies are managed by the respective State Election Commissions, not directly by the ECI.

questions.question: Which body manages direct elections to Gram Panchayats and Urban Local Bodies at the grassroots level?
questions.explanation: State Election Commissions conduct elections to local bodies (gram panchayats and municipalities) at the grassroots level.

questions.question: At the national level, the Election Commission of India consists of:
options: One Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners
One Chief Election Commissioner and five Election Commissioners
questions.explanation: At the national level, the ECI comprises the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and two Election Commissioners.

questions.question: Who heads the election machinery at the State or Union Territory level?
questions.explanation: At the State/UT level, the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) oversees electoral operations under the ECI.

questions.question: At the district level, who is the senior official overseeing the election apparatus?
questions.explanation: The District Election Officer (DEO) manages election administration at the district level, assisted by ROs and EROs.

questions.question: What is the specific responsibility of a Returning Officer (RO)?
questions.explanation: As shown in Fig. 5.11, the Returning Officer (RO) is responsible for conducting elections in a constituency.

questions.question: Which official is specifically responsible for managing and updating the voter list (electoral roll)?
questions.explanation: The Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) manages the voter list (electoral roll) at the district/constituency level.

questions.question: Where is the main office (headquarters) of the Election Commission of India located?
questions.explanation: The headquarters of the Election Commission of India (Nirvachan Sadan) is located in Delhi.

questions.question: Which of the following is a core task performed by the Election Commission of India?
options: Setting election dates, registering political parties, and enforcing the Model Code of Conduct
questions.explanation: The ECI sets election dates, enforces the Model Code of Conduct, registers political parties, and oversees the entire electoral process.

questions.question: Which of the following complete sets of elections is conducted by the Election Commission of India?
options: Municipalities, Zila Parishads, and State Assemblies
Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, and Gram Panchayats
Only Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, President, and Vice President
questions.explanation: The ECI conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and the offices of the President and Vice President.

questions.question: Besides permanent ECI staff, who are commonly deployed across India to assist in conducting elections at polling stations?
questions.explanation: Because managing over 1 million polling stations is a mammoth task, large numbers of personnel—including school teachers—are deployed for election duty.

questions.question: Arrange the ECI administrative hierarchy from the highest (national) level down to the district/constituency level:
questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs from National level (Chief Election Commissioner & 2 ECs) → State/UT level (Chief Electoral Officer) → District level (District Election Officer) → Returning Officer & Electoral Registration Officer.

questions.question: What is the full form of EVM?
questions.explanation: EVM stands for Electronic Voting Machine, used across India for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections.

questions.question: What is the full form of VVPAT?
questions.explanation: VVPAT stands for Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, which prints a physical paper slip allowing voters to verify their vote.

questions.question: Inside a polling station, what is the duty of the 1st Polling Officer?
options: Pressing the button on the EVM
Checking the voter's name on the voter list and verifying ID proof
Collecting the voter chit and checking the inked finger
Inking the voter's finger and taking their signature
questions.explanation: The 1st Polling Officer verifies the voter's name on the electoral roll (voter list) and checks their ID proof.

questions.question: What task is performed by the 2nd Polling Officer at a polling booth?
options: Checking the voter's name on the electoral roll
Taking the chit and activating the EVM
Inking the voter's finger, giving a chit, and taking the voter's signature
questions.explanation: The 2nd Polling Officer applies indelible ink on the voter's finger, issues a voter chit, and records the voter's signature.

questions.question: What does the 3rd Polling Officer do just before the voter proceeds to the EVM compartment?
options: Takes the chit and checks the voter's inked finger
Hands over the VVPAT slip to take home
Applies ink on the voter's finger
questions.explanation: The 3rd Polling Officer collects the chit issued by the 2nd officer, inspects the inked finger, and enables the ballot unit for voting.

questions.question: How does a voter confirm that their vote has been recorded after pressing the candidate's button on the EVM?
options: They hear a beep sound and verify the printed slip visible in the VVPAT machine
The polling officer announces the candidate's name
A paper receipt is handed to them to take home
They receive an SMS on their phone
questions.explanation: Upon pressing the button on the EVM, a beep sounds and the VVPAT displays a printed slip showing the chosen candidate's details before dropping into a sealed box.

questions.question: Why is indelible ink applied to a voter's finger at the polling station?
options: To mark which party the voter supported
To prevent a person from voting more than once in the same election
questions.explanation: Indelible ink marks that the citizen has already cast their vote, preventing duplicate or fraudulent voting.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of the VVPAT system alongside EVMs?
options: It creates a physical paper record for voter verification and backup recounting in case of disputes
It allows voters to change their vote the next day
It replaces the need for polling officers
It connects EVMs to the internet
questions.explanation: VVPAT produces a physical paper audit trail so voters can verify their vote and officials have a backup for verification or recounting if disputes arise.

questions.question: Which two countries are specifically mentioned in the NCERT chapter as having used India's EVM and VVPAT systems with support from the ECI?
questions.explanation: India's EVMs and VVPAT systems have been used in Namibia and Bhutan with support from the Election Commission of India.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of EVMs over traditional paper ballots?
options: They are faster to count, more accurate, and eco-friendly
They require cutting down more trees
They reveal the voter's identity publicly
They eliminate the need for constituencies
questions.explanation: EVMs reduce paper waste (eco-friendly), eliminate invalid/smudged ballot marks, and make vote counting much faster and more accurate.

questions.question: Which document is commonly issued by the ECI as proof of voter registration?
questions.explanation: The Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC), commonly called the Voter ID card, serves as official proof of voter registration.

questions.question: Can a citizen vote on election day if their name is NOT registered in the electoral roll?
options: Yes, if a candidate signs for them
Yes, only in Lok Sabha elections
Yes, by showing any school ID
No, voter registration in the constituency's electoral roll is mandatory
questions.explanation: To exercise the right to vote, an eligible citizen must be registered on the electoral roll (voter list) of their constituency.

questions.question: Where is the NOTA button located during Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections?
options: On the EVM ballot unit alongside the candidates' buttons
questions.explanation: NOTA (None Of The Above) is provided as an option directly on the EVM ballot unit.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of steps for a voter inside an Indian polling booth?
options: Give chit → Check voter list → Press EVM → Ink finger
Check voter list & ID → Ink finger, get chit & sign → Give chit & finger check → Press EVM & check VVPAT
Press EVM → Ink finger → Check voter list → Sign register
Ink finger → Check voter list → Press EVM → Submit chit
questions.explanation: Step 1: 1st officer checks voter list & ID; Step 2: 2nd officer inks finger, gives chit & takes signature; Step 3: 3rd officer takes chit & checks finger; Step 4: Press EVM button & check VVPAT slip.

questions.question: Can a voter take the VVPAT printed slip home as proof of whom they voted for?
options: Yes, if the 3rd polling officer permits
Only senior citizens can take it home
No, it stays inside a sealed compartment of the VVPAT machine to preserve secret ballot
questions.explanation: The VVPAT slip is visible through a glass window for a few seconds and then drops into a sealed drop box, preserving the secrecy of the vote.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: What is the main purpose of the Model Code of Conduct (MCC)?
options: To decide salaries of elected MPs
To list dos and don'ts for political parties, leaders, and candidates to ensure free and fair elections
questions.explanation: The Model Code of Conduct sets rules of conduct for leaders, political parties, and candidates to ensure peaceful, free, and fair elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: In which Indian state and year was the Model Code of Conduct first voluntarily adopted by major political parties?
questions.explanation: The Model Code of Conduct was first adopted in Kerala in 1960, voluntarily approved by representatives of major political parties.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: During which general elections did the ECI first circulate the Model Code of Conduct to political parties?
questions.explanation: Following Kerala's 1960 initiative, the ECI circulated the Model Code of Conduct to political parties during the 1962 general elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: From which year did the Election Commission of India become proactive in strictly ensuring the observance of the Model Code of Conduct?
questions.explanation: From 1991 onwards, the ECI became proactive in strictly enforcing the observance of the Model Code of Conduct.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Under the Model Code of Conduct, why is the party in government barred from announcing new schemes or projects once elections are announced?
options: To save money for foreign travel
To prevent the ruling party from using government resources to unfairly influence voters
questions.explanation: The MCC ensures a level playing field by prohibiting the ruling party from using official government resources or announcing new schemes to sway voters.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: A candidate distributes sarees and household appliances to voters before polling day. This is a violation of:
options: Model Code of Conduct (bribery / influencing voters with gifts)
questions.explanation: Influencing voters through gifts such as sarees, appliances, or cash in return for votes is strictly prohibited and punishable under the MCC.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: During election inspections, bundles of ₹500 notes are discovered in a candidate's car. What issue does this represent?
options: Illegal use of money power to bribe voters, violating the MCC
questions.explanation: Carrying unaccounted cash bundles to distribute to voters violates the MCC and reflects the challenge of money power in elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Why is it a violation of the Model Code of Conduct for government officials to campaign for the ruling party?
options: Government machinery must remain neutral and cannot be misused to favour any political party
Government officials are not allowed to vote
Only teachers are allowed to campaign
Campaigning is banned for all citizens
questions.explanation: Government officials must stay impartial during elections; using official machinery to campaign for the ruling party violates the MCC.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Using abusive language against an opposing candidate during election rallies violates which requirement of the MCC?
options: Discretion and restraint to ensure peaceful and respectful elections
questions.explanation: All candidates are expected to exercise discretion and restraint so that elections remain peaceful and dignified.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: In which year did T.N. Seshan become the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan became the Chief Election Commissioner in 1990 and transformed the ECI into a fearless, strict guardian of free and fair elections.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which major reform did T.N. Seshan introduce to eliminate proxy voting (fake voting on someone else's behalf)?
options: Replacing Lok Sabha with Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan championed the introduction of Voter ID cards specifically to eliminate proxy voting and bogus votes.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which of the following sets of electoral reforms is associated with former Chief Election Commissioner T.N. Seshan?
options: Creating State Election Commissions and Panchayati Raj
Precise campaigning rules, Voter IDs to stop proxy voting, and strict vigilance on candidate spending
Lowering voting age to 18 and introducing NOTA
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan enforced strict campaigning rules, introduced Voter IDs to curb proxy voting, and maintained strict vigilance over candidate expenditure.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Who is responsible for enforcing the Model Code of Conduct during Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections?
questions.explanation: Enforcing the Model Code of Conduct and handling complaints of violations is one of the core functions of the ECI.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which of the following actions IS permitted during election campaigning under the Model Code of Conduct?
options: Peacefully presenting a party's manifesto and policies to voters
Using government vehicles for party rallies
questions.explanation: Candidates and parties are free to peacefully explain their manifestos, promises, and policies without bribing, abusing, or misusing government resources.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Why is T.N. Seshan widely remembered in Indian electoral history?
options: He was India's first voter in 1951
He invented the Electronic Voting Machine
He drafted Article 326 in the Constituent Assembly
He made Indian elections fairer, more transparent, and fearless through strict enforcement of rules
questions.explanation: T.N. Seshan worked relentlessly to protect voters' rights and is remembered as the officer who made Indian elections fairer, transparent, and fearless.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What joyful phrase is often used to describe elections in India?
questions.explanation: Elections in India are often celebrated as the 'Festival of Democracy', when citizens freely and responsibly choose their representatives.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Into how many parliamentary constituencies is India divided for Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: India is divided into 543 parliamentary constituencies for elections to the Lok Sabha.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Out of the 543 Lok Sabha constituencies, how many seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) respectively?
questions.explanation: Of the 543 Lok Sabha seats, 84 are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC), 47 for Scheduled Tribes (ST), and 412 are General seats.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How many General (unreserved) constituencies are there in the 543-member Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation: 543 total constituencies minus 84 SC and 47 ST reserved seats equals 412 General constituencies.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which electoral system is used for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections in India?
questions.explanation: India uses the First-Past-The-Post system for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections, where the candidate securing the most votes in a constituency wins.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the key difference between an MP and an MLA?
options: MPs represent citizens in the national Parliament, while MLAs represent citizens in the State Legislative Assembly
MLAs focus on foreign policy while MPs run village panchayats
Only MPs are chosen by universal adult franchise
MPs are appointed while MLAs are elected
questions.explanation: Members of Parliament (MPs) represent people in the national Parliament on national issues, whereas Members of Legislative Assembly (MLAs) represent them in State Assemblies on regional issues.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: By what regional names is the State Legislative Assembly known in different parts of India?
questions.explanation: The State Legislative Assembly is known by regional names such as Vidhan Sabha (e.g., in Hindi-speaking states) and Niyama Sabha (e.g., in Kerala).

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is a 'coalition' in the context of government formation?
options: A single party winning all seats
A group of two or more political parties working together to form a majority
A merger of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: A coalition is an alliance of two or more political parties working together, often to achieve a majority of seats and form the government.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Who typically becomes the Prime Minister of India and the Chief Minister of a state respectively?
options: The leaders of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha and in the State Assembly
The seniormost judges of the Supreme Court and High Court
The winners of the Rajya Sabha and Panchayat elections
The appointees of the Election Commission
questions.explanation: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha typically becomes the Prime Minister, while the majority leader in a State Assembly becomes the Chief Minister.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How are the 245 members of the Rajya Sabha chosen?
options: 200 are elected by MPs and 45 by Governors
All 245 are nominated by the Prime Minister
233 are indirectly elected by MLAs of State Legislative Assemblies, and 12 are nominated by the President
All 245 are directly elected by voters
questions.explanation: Of the 245 Rajya Sabha members, 233 are indirectly elected by elected MLAs of states/UTs and 12 distinguished individuals are nominated by the President of India.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Why is the Rajya Sabha called the 'Permanent House'?
options: Because it is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years
Because its members serve for life
Because its building is older than the Lok Sabha
Because it meets every single day of the year
questions.explanation: The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved; instead, one-third of its members retire every two years and new members are elected, ensuring continuity.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the normal term of a member of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.explanation: Each member of the Rajya Sabha serves a six-year term, with one-third retiring every two years.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: On what basis are Rajya Sabha seats allotted to different Indian states?
options: Number of districts in the state
Equal seats for every state regardless of size
Population of the state (more populous states like Uttar Pradesh have more seats than Arunachal Pradesh)
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha seat allocation is based on state population—for example, Uttar Pradesh has far more seats than less populous states like Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which voting system is used in Rajya Sabha elections to ensure fair representation for smaller states and proportional voices?
questions.explanation: MLAs vote in Rajya Sabha elections using the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system, ranking candidates by preference.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What does the term 'dissolution' mean in relation to a legislative house?
options: Expiry or termination of a house due to the end of its term or other Constitutional reason
Suspending a single member for one day
questions.explanation: Dissolution means the expiry or termination of a legislative body (such as the Lok Sabha) due to the end of its term or another Constitutional reason.

questions.question: How is the President of India elected?
questions.explanation: The President of India is elected indirectly by an Electoral College representing both the Union Parliament and State/UT legislatures.

questions.question: Who constitutes the Electoral College that elects the President of India?
options: Elected MPs of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha + Elected MLAs of all States and UTs of Delhi and Puducherry
Only Lok Sabha MPs and Governors
Only Chief Ministers of all States
All elected and nominated MPs and MLAs
questions.explanation: The President's Electoral College consists of elected MPs of both Houses of Parliament and elected MLAs of all States plus the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry.

questions.question: Which of the following groups IS NOT allowed to vote in the election of the President of India?
options: Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry
Elected MPs of the Rajya Sabha
Members of State Legislative Councils (MLCs) and nominated MPs/MLAs
Elected MPs of the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: Nominated Rajya Sabha MPs (12), nominated MLAs, nominated UT members, and all Members of Legislative Councils (both elected and nominated) do not participate in the Presidential election.

questions.question: Why are nominated members excluded from voting in the election of the President of India?
options: Because they do not attend Parliament
Because they already vote in Vice President elections
Because they are not Indian citizens
To ensure that only elected representatives vote, maintaining democratic legitimacy
questions.explanation: Excluding nominated members ensures that the President is elected solely by elected representatives, preserving indirect democratic legitimacy.

questions.question: What is a 'bicameral legislature'?
options: A legislature with only two political parties
A legislature elected every two years
A legislature divided into two separate chambers or houses
A legislature that meets twice a year
questions.explanation: A bicameral legislature has two separate chambers or houses (e.g., Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha at the Union level, or Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council in certain states).

questions.question: Which voting system is used for electing both the President and the Vice President of India?
questions.explanation: Both the President and Vice President of India are elected indirectly using the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system.

questions.question: How does the Electoral College for the Vice President of India differ from that of the President?
options: Only Lok Sabha MPs vote for the Vice President
All adult citizens vote directly for the Vice President
Both elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament vote, and State MLAs do NOT participate
Only State MLAs vote for the Vice President
questions.explanation: The Vice President is elected by both elected and nominated members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; State MLAs do not vote in the Vice Presidential election.

questions.question: Who serves as the Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha?
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: The Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: Who steps in to discharge the functions of the President of India if the President is unable to perform their duties?
questions.explanation: When the President is unable to discharge their functions, the Vice President steps in to perform the role.

questions.question: Which two Union Territories' elected MLAs participate in the Electoral College for the President of India (as listed in the NCERT chapter)?
options: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu
questions.explanation: The NCERT chapter specifically notes that elected MLAs of all Indian states and the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry are part of the President's Electoral College.

questions.question: Which three major challenges to India's electoral system are highlighted in the 'Challenges and The Road Ahead' section of the chapter?
options: Growing influence of money, candidates with criminal records, and voter apathy (especially in urban areas)
Low population, lack of languages, and too many holidays
Lack of paper, short election terms, and too few parties
Shortage of polling booths, absence of EVMs, and ban on campaigning
questions.explanation: The textbook identifies money power in elections, candidates with criminal records, and voter apathy (particularly in urban areas) as key challenges.

questions.question: Where is 'voter apathy' (low willingness to come out and vote) noted as being particularly concerning in India?
questions.explanation: The NCERT chapter specifically highlights declining voter turnout and voter apathy particularly in urban areas.

questions.question: According to the NCERT chapter, what is 'the strongest safeguard of a democratic system'?
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes that 'an aware and vigilant voter is the strongest safeguard of a democratic system'—starting with asking the right questions and ending with casting a responsible vote.

questions.question: Which combination of forces must work together to empower voters—especially youth—to make thoughtful electoral choices?
questions.explanation: Media, education, and awareness campaigns must work together to inform citizens, particularly youth, about voting wisely and responsibly.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a DIRECT election and an INDIRECT election in India?
options: Direct: Vice President | Indirect: Gram Panchayat
Direct: Lok Sabha & State Assembly | Indirect: Rajya Sabha, President & Vice President
Direct: President of India | Indirect: State Legislative Assembly
Direct: Rajya Sabha | Indirect: Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies, and local bodies are chosen through direct elections by citizens, whereas Rajya Sabha, President, and Vice President are chosen through indirect elections.

questions.question: Assertion (A): India adopted Universal Adult Franchise immediately after Independence despite a 14% literacy rate. Reason (R): The Constitution makers believed every adult citizen is equal and capable of participating in democracy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Despite only ~14% literacy in 1947, the Constitution makers had 'abundant faith in the common man' and granted equal voting rights to all adult citizens.

questions.question: Which word is a direct synonym of 'franchise' as mentioned in the NCERT Class 8 Civics chapter?
questions.explanation: The textbook explicitly defines 'suffrage' as a synonym of 'franchise', both meaning the right to vote.

questions.question: Can an elderly parent legally authorize their adult son or daughter to go to the polling booth and cast a vote on their behalf?
options: Yes, if both share the same address
Yes, only in State Assembly elections
No, under Universal Adult Franchise no one can vote on another person's behalf
questions.explanation: No one can vote on another's behalf; instead, the ECI offers home voting and accessibility assistance so elderly citizens can vote themselves.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the NCERT mindmap (Fig. 5.4) as a reason why Universal Adult Franchise is vital for democracy?
options: Guarantees that only one political party remains in power
Elected representatives remain answerable to the electorate
questions.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise promotes equality, civic engagement, and accountability—never one-party rule.

questions.question: Before 1988, what was the minimum age required to cast a vote in Indian elections?
questions.explanation: Originally, the minimum voting age in India was 21 years; it was lowered to 18 years in 1988.

questions.question: In the 10th-century Uttaramerur selection process, who physically drew the palm leaves from the sealed pot?
questions.explanation: On selection day, the sealed pot was opened publicly and a young boy drew the palm leaves randomly one by one to ensure impartiality.

questions.question: If about 34% of eligible voters did NOT vote in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, approximately what percentage of eligible voters DID cast their vote?
questions.explanation: Since roughly 34% of eligible voters did not exercise their franchise in 2024, approximately 66% participated in voting.

questions.question: At what age was India's first voter, Shyam Saran Negi, photographed casting his vote in 2017 in the NCERT textbook?
questions.explanation: Fig. 5.15 shows Shyam Saran Negi (first voter in 1951) casting his vote in 2017 at the age of 100.

questions.question: How can persons with disabilities request wheelchairs or assistance at polling booths according to the NCERT chapter?
options: Only by writing to the Supreme Court
Through app-based requests for assistance provided by the ECI
questions.explanation: The ECI enables app-based requests for assistance, including wheelchairs and ramps, alongside Braille-enabled voter cards.

questions.question: Why does the NCERT chapter compare India's voter population with the UK and India's area with France?
options: To illustrate the massive scale and geographical complexity of organising Indian elections
To show that India copies their election laws
To prove France has more voters than India
To explain why India does not need polling stations
questions.explanation: India has 15× the UK's population in eligible voters and 6× France's area, demonstrating why an elaborate electoral system is essential.

questions.question: In the Suryodaya School election, how many valid votes were counted out of the 33 ballots cast?
questions.explanation: Ahmed got 8, Gurmat got 12, and Ravi got 10 (total 30 counted votes in the caselet), with unmarked ballots declared invalid.

questions.question: Which symbol were Grade 8 students at Suryodaya School asked to mark next to their chosen candidate's name on the ballot paper?
questions.explanation: Students marked an 'X' next to the candidate's name on the paper ballot without writing their own name, preserving secrecy.

questions.question: If NOTA receives more votes than any candidate in a constituency, what happens to the election result as per India's current system?
options: The constituency remains empty for 5 years
The candidate with the highest number of votes among contestants still wins; NOTA does not change the result
questions.explanation: The NCERT chapter clarifies that NOTA does not change the election result, but acts as a quiet, powerful message that voters want better choices.

questions.question: Why is the independence of the Election Commission of India essential for democracy?
options: So it can favour the ruling party during campaigns
So it can appoint state Chief Ministers
So it can make laws instead of Parliament
So elections are conducted freely and fairly without interference from the government or any political party
questions.explanation: Being an independent constitutional body ensures the ECI can enforce rules impartially even against the party currently in government.

questions.question: Match the ECI official with their correct level: (1) Chief Election Commissioner, (2) Chief Electoral Officer, (3) District Election Officer.
questions.explanation: CEC (with 2 ECs) operates at the National level, CEO at the State/UT level, and DEO at the District level.

questions.question: In conducting local body elections at the grassroots level, how do State Election Commissions work with the ECI?
options: They manage local body elections in consultation with the ECI, following all Constitutional provisions for direct elections
They report only to political parties
questions.explanation: State Election Commissions conduct grassroots local body elections in consultation with the ECI, upholding universal adult franchise.

questions.question: Which polling officer at a booth is responsible for taking the voter's signature after applying ink on their finger?
questions.explanation: The 2nd Polling Officer inks the voter's finger, hands over the voter chit, and takes the voter's signature.

questions.question: What auditory cue confirms that your button press on an Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) has been registered?
options: A voice recording of the candidate
A bell rung by the 1st polling officer
questions.explanation: Pressing the button on the EVM produces a beep sound, accompanied by the printed slip appearing in the VVPAT window.

questions.question: Why does the VVPAT paper trail remain crucial even when electronic voting machines are fast and accurate?
options: It provides a physical backup for verification and recounting in case of disputes or electronic failures
It lets candidates see who voted for them
It prints voter ID cards at the booth
questions.explanation: VVPAT builds public trust by allowing instant voter verification and serving as a physical audit backup for recounting.

questions.question: Which international role has the Election Commission of India played regarding EVM and VVPAT technology?
options: Keeping the technology completely secret from all nations
Supporting countries like Namibia and Bhutan and training other nations interested in adopting it
questions.explanation: India's EVMs and VVPATs have been used in Namibia and Bhutan with ECI support, and several other countries have received training from India.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Arrange these milestones in the history of India's Model Code of Conduct in chronological order: (I) Proactive ECI enforcement, (II) Voluntary adoption in Kerala, (III) Circulated by ECI in general elections.
questions.explanation: Kerala voluntarily adopted MCC in 1960 (II), the ECI circulated it during the 1962 general elections (III), and became proactive in enforcing it from 1991 (I).

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: A State Chief Minister announces a brand-new free laptop scheme two days after election dates are declared. Under the MCC, this action is:
options: A violation of the Model Code of Conduct, as no new schemes may be announced to influence voters
Allowed because they are still Chief Minister
questions.explanation: Once the MCC takes effect, the party in government cannot announce new schemes or projects that may influence voters.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: What does 'proxy voting' mean, which T.N. Seshan fought to eliminate using Voter ID cards?
options: Someone else illegally casting a vote in another registered voter's name
Voting from home with ECI approval
questions.explanation: Proxy/impersonation voting occurs when one person votes fraudulently in another's name; photo Voter IDs were introduced to stop it.

questions.topic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) & T.N. Seshan
questions.question: Which of the following is a complaint the ECI handles as a Model Code of Conduct violation?
options: Cash bundles found in a candidate's car or gifts distributed to voters
A voter pressing the NOTA button
A school teacher performing election duty
A voter checking their name on the voter list
questions.explanation: Figs. 5.17–5.20 highlight distributing gifts, abusive speech, officials campaigning, and unaccounted cash bundles as MCC violations.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Why are 84 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and 47 seats for Scheduled Tribes (ST) in the Lok Sabha?
options: To reduce the total number of constituencies
To increase the term of the Lok Sabha
To ensure historically marginalised and disadvantaged communities have fair representation in Parliament
Because SCs and STs cannot vote in General constituencies
questions.explanation: Reserved constituencies ensure adequate political representation for historically marginalised SC and ST communities in Parliament.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the relationship between a Lok Sabha constituency and State Assembly constituencies?
options: They are always identical in size across India
A single Lok Sabha constituency may contain two or more State Assembly constituencies
Lok Sabha constituencies exist only in Delhi
Every State Assembly constituency contains 5 Lok Sabha constituencies
questions.explanation: As noted in the chapter's 'Let's Explore' box, one parliamentary (Lok Sabha) constituency typically encompasses two or more smaller assembly constituencies.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Which house of Parliament focuses on national issues and is directly elected by citizens as the 'Lower House'?
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha is the Lower House of Parliament, directly elected by voters across 543 constituencies to address national issues.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: Every two years, what fraction of Rajya Sabha members retire so that new members can be elected?
questions.explanation: One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years, keeping it a continuous Permanent House that is never dissolved.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India?
questions.explanation: The President of India nominates 12 distinguished individuals to the 245-member Rajya Sabha, while 233 are elected by MLAs.

questions.topic: Lok Sabha, State Assemblies & Rajya Sabha
questions.question: What is the other constitutional name of the Rajya Sabha shown in Fig. 5.23?
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha is also called the Council of States (Upper House), representing India's states and union territories.

questions.question: Why does the President's Electoral College include both Union MPs and State/UT MLAs?
options: To make the election faster than FPTP
Because MLAs cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections
Because there are too few MPs in Delhi
Because the President represents the whole country, ensuring support of both central and state governments
questions.explanation: Including elected MPs and elected MLAs ensures the President enjoys the democratic support of both the Union and the States.

questions.question: In states with a bicameral legislature (Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council), who can vote in the election of the President of India?
options: Only elected MLAs (Members of Legislative Councils — both elected and nominated — are excluded)
questions.explanation: Members of Legislative Councils (both elected and nominated) are explicitly excluded from the President's Electoral College.

questions.question: Can the 12 nominated members of the Rajya Sabha vote in the election of the Vice President of India?
options: Yes, the Vice President's Electoral College includes both elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament
No, nominated members never vote in any election
Only if the Prime Minister permits them
questions.explanation: Unlike the Presidential election, the Vice President's Electoral College includes BOTH elected and nominated members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: Do Members of State Legislative Assemblies (MLAs) participate in electing the Vice President of India?
options: No, only members of both Houses of Parliament vote for the Vice President
Only MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry vote
questions.explanation: State MLAs participate in electing the President, but NOT the Vice President—who is elected solely by MPs of both Houses of Parliament.

questions.question: In the Presidential election, why do more populous states have a greater say in the Electoral College?
options: Because populous states get to nominate 12 MPs each
Because their MLAs cast open voice votes
Because the elaborate voting and counting rules weight representation according to state population
questions.explanation: The textbook notes that Presidential voting and counting rules are elaborate so that more populous states have a proportionally greater say.

questions.question: Which of the following is a potential challenge of social media during elections discussed in the chapter's activities?
options: It completely stops young people from hearing speeches
While it spreads awareness, catchy reels and misinformation can also confuse voters
questions.explanation: Social media boosts youth engagement and access to information, but can also spread misleading content or confusion if voters are not vigilant.

questions.question: According to the NCERT chapter, why is the right to vote also called a 'responsibility'?
options: Because every citizen must stay informed, ask the right questions, and vote thoughtfully for democracy to succeed
Because voters must campaign for a party
Because voters must pay a fee to vote
Because only responsible officers can vote
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that voting is both a right and a responsibility requiring voter awareness, vigilance, and thoughtful choice.

questions.question: Which website is suggested at the end of the NCERT chapter for exploring past parliamentary and assembly constituency election results?
questions.explanation: Question 9 of the chapter's 'Questions and activities' invites students to explore constituency results on https://www.indiavotes.com.

questions.question: Compare the three indirect elections covered in Chapter 5: Rajya Sabha, President, and Vice President. What voting system do ALL THREE share?
options: Direct secret ballot by all 18+ citizens
questions.explanation: All three indirect elections—Rajya Sabha MPs, the President, and the Vice President—use the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system.

questions.question: Complete the NCERT chapter's concluding democratic principle: 'It starts with asking the right questions — and ends with...'
questions.explanation: The chapter closes with the memorable line: 'It starts with asking the right questions — and ends with casting a responsible vote.'
